title: Ports, Sockets, and Scanning Your Own Hosts
intro: What's actually exposed on your servers is often different from what you think is exposed. Checking from the inside (what's listening) and the outside (what's reachable) catches both mistakes and leftovers.

steps.prompt: Find which process is using port 3000.
steps.fake_output:
COMMAND  PID  USER   FD  TYPE  DEVICE  NODE NAME
node    4821 appsvc 21u IPv4 81234   TCP *:3000 (LISTEN)
steps.explanation: A node process, owned by appsvc, is listening on all interfaces.
steps.why: lsof and 'ss -tulnp' answer the same question from different angles. lsof also shows established connections and files, which helps when you need to know who is connected TO a port, not just who is listening on it.

steps.prompt: From another machine, scan the first 1000 ports of web01 (a server you own) to see what's reachable from the network.
steps.fake_output:
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp   open     ssh
80/tcp   open     http
443/tcp  open     https
111/tcp  open     rpcbind

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up)
steps.explanation: rpcbind on 111 is open to the network — almost certainly unintended on a web server.
steps.why: Only scan hosts you own or are authorized to test — scanning others' systems can violate policy or law. Scanning your own from outside catches services that are listening on 0.0.0.0 by default and should have been firewalled or disabled.

steps.prompt: Identify exactly what software and version is behind each open port.
steps.fake_output:
PORT    STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu
80/tcp  open  http    nginx 1.18.0
111/tcp open  rpcbind 2-4 (RPC #100000)
steps.explanation: -sV probes each service to fingerprint its version.
steps.why: This is exactly what an attacker's first recon step looks like — outdated versions stand out immediately. It's also a good argument for hiding version banners (e.g. nginx's server_tokens off).

steps.prompt: Check the HTTP status code of the web service without printing the page body — a quick health check you can script.
steps.explanation: Just the status code, nothing else.
steps.why: Perfect for shell scripts and cron health checks: compare the output to 200 and alert otherwise, without parsing HTML or JSON.
